ROCHE (Marquette) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 74) respecting representation in the North-west Territories. He said :	Mr. Speaker, I
would ask leave to change the title of this Bill from one to amend the Dominion Elections Act, 1900. to a Bill to amend the Act respecting representation in the North-west Territories.
Explain.

This Bill refers solely to the North-west Territories, and it
is meant to correct certain abuses which crept in during the last election. For instance, the lists in the North-west Territories are supposed to be completed and posted up eight (Jays prior to election day, and to be finally revised two days prior to election day. The enumerators who prepare the lists also revise them and it has occurred that political opponents, desiring to obtain certificates for voters to poll their votes outside of their own polling subdivisions, have been unable to do so until within two days of an election day, whereas political friends have been enabled to obtain certificates any time within eight days. The Bill contains a clause to correct this abuse and to allow the issue of certificates any time during the eight days and also to provide a penalty for issuing blank certificates. Blank certificates have been issued to friends, whereas they have been refused to opponents, and a clause has been introduced to correct that. Then, again, the enumerator who would not give any certificates to his political opponents until within two days of the election would conveniently make himself scarce during these two days, and our friends were not able to obtain certificates at all. A clause has been introduced into the Bill settling the place, or office, where this enumerator may be found in order to secure certificates and to have placed on the list names that are entitled to be there. It also provides penalties for the wilful infraction of any of these provisions. These, in short, are the amendments proposed, which will be explained more in detail upon the second reading of the Bill.	.

May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Marquette) if that can be made applicable to, say, the province of Manitoba, particularly in regard to requiring that the returning officer should have an office in which he may be found before the election ? I was utterly unable to get any certificates because he absented himself for four days.
That can be provided for, but it is not included in this Bill, which applies only to the North-west Territories.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Mr. EDWARD HACKETT (West Prince, P.E.I.) Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of tlie Day are entered into, I desire to bring to the notice of the government a very urgent matter affecting the people of Canada. It especially affects the people of Prince Edward Island, and when I say the people of Prince Edward Island I mean the people of Canada. I regret that I am unable to give notice of this question, but I want to ask the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) : How are the trains down in Prince Edward Island moving ? What means has he taken to see that the people there are supplied with train accommodation that they should be supplied with ?
If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) wants to enter into a discussion he will have to move the adjournment of the House. If it is only to ask a question upon an urgent matter
I do not wish to go into a discussion.
I would ask the hon. gentleman simply to put his question without engaging in a debate.

I move that the House do now adjourn in order to put myself in order. The people of Prince Edward Island paid for that railway. It cost them $3,250,000. At the time of confederation that railway became the property of Canada and it was to be operated by the government of Canada. I have never known since confederation that the government of Canada has failed in its duty in operating that railway. But, I hold in my hand a telegram, received by me to-day from a friend in Prince Edward Island. I will read that telegram to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and I am pleased to see that he is present and that the time is most opportune now to reply to this question.
Mr. Edward Hackett, M.P., Ottawa :
Tignish, P.E.I., March 15, 1901. No train this week. Superintendent won't employ sufficient men clear track.
(Sgd.) P. C. MURPHY. M.D.

That Is all. The Minister of Railways will not employ the men to shovel the track although plenty of men are to be found to do the work. In the interest of the people whom I represent, I ask the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) to see that they shall have at least one train a day. We find the people of western Canada agitating for railway accommodation in Manitoba and the North-west and elsewhere where we are building railways, and the people of Prince Edward Island are satisfied that they shall have all necessary accommodation notwithstanding that in the Mr. HACKETT.
little province we are deprived of anything like a decent mail service. The urgency of the matter will be seen when this gentleman to whom I referred, had to pay an extra amount for the sending of his telegram across the short cable of nine miles, from Cape Traverse to Cape Tormentine. I, as the representative of my constituents ask the Minister of Railways, I call on him and I demand from him that he shall see that sufficient men are employed to keep the track clear and give the people west of Summerside that railway accommodation they are entitled to.

The information which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hack-ett) has just now given me is the first I have had on this subject, and I think it would perhaps have sufficed if the hon. gentleman had sent me the telegram and put me in possession of the information which he has, so that I could have communicated with the general manager and j have the matter inquired into. I am quite sure that there is no disposition on the part of any of the authorities to stay their hands when obstacles occur in connection with the running of our trains. The mere employment of additional labour would not, I am sure, prompt them to refuse doing anything that might be required under such circumstances. They have no instructions which would warrant them in not giving a proper service to any part of the Island, or indeed any other portion of the government railways. If the hon. gentleman will send me that telegram I will at once communicate with Moncton and ascertain what the facts are. I am not at all surprised that trains should be blocked there, because that is not an uncommon thing when storms are heavy and the same thing is occurring all over Canada. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) that perhaps those who are writing or inspiring such newspaper articles as he has read are more anxious to find a grievance and make a complaint than they are to bring the facts to the knowledge of the proper officers. I would suspect that the paper that the hon. gentleman has read from, is not one which is ordinarily friendly to the government, and I would imagine that it was not anxious to put the case in an impartial way. There is certainlv no design on the part of the Minister of Railways or of the government, or the department to refuse the people nil nroper railway facilities or accommodation. I promise the hon. gentleman that I will inquire into the matter at once. 1 am advised that the very paper which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) has read from, contains the additional statement that the condition which is represented to have occurred on tile western portion of the line lias occurred all over the line. The hon. gentle-
man (Mr. Hackett) will know whether that is correct or not. If it is correct, it will show that this block in the west is not due to any discrimination on the part of the authorities.

speechtext:
Before the Orders of the Day are called, will the right hon. the Prime Minister permit me to mention that I have just received a telegram from the president of the Board of Trade of Halifax protesting against a contract being made with the Manchester line which omits Halifax as a port of call on the homeward voyage. The board protests that the subsidy should not be granted unless Halifax is included both ways, and stipulation made that Halifax shippers shall have the privilege of shipping at least
2,000	tons per homeward voyage. I presume that the matter has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), but in case it has not, I take the opportunity of mentioning it now. It is a matter which demands the attention of the minister.

The House resumed adjourned debate on the proposed motion of Hon. Mr. Fielding :
That Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into committee to consider of the Ways and Means for raising the Supply to he granted to His Majesty.
['Very well.']

Mr. Speaker, it is always matter of honest and legitimate curiosity on the advent of a new parliament, to ascertain whether either of the great parties representing the two great divisions of public opinion in this country have anything in the way of a new policy to propose ; and when, as in the case of one of these we have the happiness of knowing that they have almost a complete brand-new outfit of new leaders the curiosity is deepened. On the present occasion, however, if I am to judge from the speech of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier), who, I suppose was constituted the mouthpiece of the opposition, and also of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) who followed him ; there does not appear to be any great chance of our legitimate curiosity being gratified. The hon. member from Toronto (Mr. Osier) in the course of his remarks yesterday observed that there was not much to be said about the budget-and the hon. member did not say much. The government largely agreeing with the hon. member (Mr. Osier), thought that they might give the opposition the great advantage always dear to theologians, to politicians, and to ladies of
all sorts and conditions, of having the last word. We were willing to rest our case on the statements of my hon. friend beside me (Hon. Mr. Fielding), thinking our friends of the opposition were likewise willing to rest their case on the champion they had provided. But as it appears that the hon. gentlemen desire a further continuation of the debate, we have no objection whatever that the matter should be discussed from every point of view.
As I have said, Sir, the hon. member for Toronto did not speak at any great length. The hon. gentleman did not give us much indication of the new policy, if a new policy there is to be, which the opposition are prepared to propound. I am bound to say that in that respect, however, although he did not speak quite as long, he gave us some more hints than the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) who succeeded him. The hon. member for Toronto is of opinion that from this time forth-I do not know whether in this he spoke for himself, or as the mouthpiece of the opposition-there should be no more bonuses to railways, unless I presume such bonuses are approved by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or some other competent authority. The hon. gentleman was likewise of opinion that the time had come when we should issue no more scrip to the half-breeds. The hon. gentleman, in the third place, thought it was' impolitic to go on expending money on the St. Lawrence navigation, if I followed him correctly, until it was pretty well established in the fulness of time whether Montreal or Quebec should be the great port of Canada. Now, Sir, if on that occasion the hon. member spoke as the mouthpiece of the opposition, and if they will formulate their views and put them in the shape of a motion embodying these three great planks, nothing will give us more pleasure than to discuss them in any way, shape or form they please to choose.
As for my hon. friend from Bothweil (Mr. Clancy), I did not observe that he made any suggestion at all, except to the effect that he was not going to be stampeded by any one-I do not know to whom he had reference-to vote .against the present preference to Great Britain unless he liked to.
In the way of criticism, the hon. member for Toronto complained at some length of the increase of the public debt. The hon. gentleman did not find it convenient to mention, what I think he might have mentioned, that in four years the total increase of the debt of Canada under the present government has been a little less than $7,000,000; while, if my memory is not at fault, in the three years preceding, the total increase of the debt of Canada had been $17,000,000. It is perfectly true that the debt of Canada increased by about $7,000,000 in the last four years; and of what items were those seven millions mainly composed ? They were composed of a grant of about

$3,500,000 to the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, a grant of $1,500,000, a free gift of the people of Canada to the troops in South Africa, and a discount of about $1,000,000 caused by the placing of a 2J per cent loan in the English market.
Mr. Speaker, I am as averse as any hon. member can be to seeing any undue increase, or any increase that can be avoided, to the public debt of this country. It is, for our means and resources, a large debt, and I do not like to see it increased; but I will say this, that in the course of my experience I never knew a case in which better value was given to the country for an addition of six or seven millions of dollars to the debt than has been given to Canada in these three items to which I have referred. By the addition of $3,500,000, In the shape of a subsidy to the Crow's Nest Pass Railway, the government very largely developed a very important region in British Columbia, and at the same time provided a large and growing market for a large section of the Northwest, a matter of great importance and value to the settlement of that country ; and it can easily be established, if hon. gentlemen choose to take the trouble to examine our records, that even at the present moment, in all human probability, the result of that expenditure and the increased population and increased trade and traffic thence accruing, has been to add to our revenue in the shape of increased returns from customs and excise, which we would not have had but for the construction of that road, a sum of money which has already almost entirely recouped the treasury of Canada for that $3,500,000. I say nothing of the importance-though they are a part of the consideration for that $3,500,-000-of the great advantages which were obtained not merely for the people of the North-west, but the people of older Canada, who are enabled to trade with British Columbia on very much better terms than they could have done if that subsidy had not been granted. For the $1,500,000 which was granted for the service of Her Majesty in South Africa, I say also that this country has obtained good and adequate value. Putting all other considerations aside, and looking at the matter from the most sordid pounds-shillings-and-pence point of view you please, as a mere mercantile venture, as an advertisement, Canada never used $1,-
500,000	to better purpose than when she sent
3,000	of her choicest troops to Africa, and when they established for themselves, as I am glad to be able to say they did, a record unsurpassed by any other portion of Her Majesty's forces, for gallantry, discipline, endurance, skill and conduct in the field. The $1,000,000 which we added to our public debt under the guise of discount on a 2i per cent loan, made by my hon. friend shortly after his entrance into office, was also money right well spent, and for this simple reason. It is a matter of very Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
great importance to us, who will have to renew our indebtedness for many millions, I think not far short of fifty or sixty millions, within the course of a few years, to establish as low a rate of interest for our loans as can possibly be obtained; and therefore that nominal addition to our debt was money very well spent and invested in the interest of the people of Canada. If my hon. friend had simply desired to keep down the apparent debt, it would have been a very easy thing for him to have floated a 3 per cent loan. Had he done so, instead of an apparent addition to our debt of $1,000,000, he would have been able to reduce It by half a million from the proceeds of the premium which he would at that period have been able to secure on such a loan. In our $200,000,000 of net debt now existing, it would be hard for any hon. gentleman to point out any case in which the people of Canada have got better value for their money than they have in these six millions which have been added to our debt under the present government. I say farther: if we were able to invest sixty millions on equally good terms, my hon. friend the Finance Minister would be well advised to do it, and do it at once.
The hon. member for Toronto also wanted to know what we had done with the large surpluses which we had received during the last few years. Sir. I am pleased to be able to inform the hon. gentleman and his friends that what we did with the surpluses to which he alludes was to pay oft' the large undischarged liabilities which our predecessors had left behind them. When we came into office we found that our predecessors had gone out of office not merely with a considerable deficit, but likewise with a large amount of undischarged liabilities.
There were several millions due on railway subsidies unpaid. There was a very large amount, not less, I think, than $10,000,000 or $12,000,000 at least, to be paid for the completion of the canal contracts which were under way and which the late government had left unfinished. If you add these sums together, you will find that there is ample scope for the employment of the entire surplus which we accumulated during our term. I say nothing of the fact, which may more fitly be discussed another time, that we had besides to turn a dead railway into a live one and provide a considerable sum for equipping and putting the Intercolonial Railway into shape to be an efficient competitor with its great rival.
But my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier), not content with the past, projected his eagle vision into the future. He desired to know what provision we were going to make for the next 25 years. I was pleased to hear that remark. The hon. gentleman is a citizen of Toronto. He has witnessed, no doubt with interest, how, for the space of thirty years, the Reform party have kept power in Ontario, and I think it suggested
itself to bis mind that as things were going there was every probability that the present party in power would be called on to provide lor the future of this country for the next 25 years. Sir, I am pleased to be able to relieve the mind of my hon. friend with respect to these 25 years. During the next 25 years, in fact, during a shorter period, we may probably have to refund the whole or very nearly the whole of our debts. At this moment, the charges for our debt and sinking fund are a little over $13,000,000 a year, but if my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) succeeds in establishing a 2J per cent or even 2J per cent rate and in dispensing with the sinking fund-as I know he will-the probabilities are that before thei 25 years will have expired, we will have reduced that $13,000,000, which is a fixed charge that we cannot control, to something like $6,000,000 or $7,000,000. And if the population-as I think, under the energetic operations of my hon. friend in front of me and other valuable members of the party, it will be-is sufficiently increased, if it resumes its normal rate of increase, and at the end of the 25 years we have 8,000,000 or 10,000,000 of people-as we have every reason to hope we may-the interest will be absolutely reduced to one-half, and, relatively to the population it will be reduced to one-quarter of the amount we now pay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright).

speechtext: Is it to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture the hon. gentleman is referring ?

My hon. colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) will answer for himself. I do not know what surprises may be in store for us, but I say candidly that I was rather sorry to see my hon. friends, who have spoken so far, were rather disposed to fall back into the old ruts. These hon. gentlemen refused-and refused, I fear, deliberately-to face the facts. They refused to admit that within the last four or five years conditions have changed to an extraordinary degree in Canada. They refused to admit that new obligations have been assumed, for which we have had to provide, and they refused entirely to make any reasonable allowance for the expenditure rendered requisite by these changed conditions. They preferred to repeat exploded charges. I had hoped better from them, I thought that those things might well enough be relegated to the limbo which always follows a general election, and that we would turn over a new leaf and deal with things to a greater extent as we find them to-day. But no doubt these hon. gentlemen, are a good deal handicapped by the traditions which they have inherited from their predecessors. No doubt also they have found it rather difficult to get anything new to propose, and they must not complain-though I notice some of them are disposed to complain- too much if the people are disposed to judge 48
them by the standards they themselves set up. I have seen a good deal of political life in Canada, and can very well recollect that, when times were hard, and we were in power, our friends opposite were the very foremost to impress on the people that these things depended entirely on the government. If times were bad the government were to blame. Sir, the people took them at their own words. The people judged them by their own standard and did, I dare say, to some extent, give my right hon. friend beside me and his colleagues credit for the fact that there were good times and that they knew how to make the most of them.
But when I come to deal with such criticisms as I have heard from hon. gentlemen opposite. I notice one thing. Not only are these criticisms to a great extent contradictory, but they appear to be self-destructive. These hon. gentlemen complain that we have stolen their policy, and almost in the same breath they complain that we introduced- especially in the matter of the preferential tariff-a totally new departure. They are never tired of complaining that we are giving England a preference, without favour or consideration granted to us, and at the same time they make it a charge against this government that one of the results of our policy has been a largely increased trade with the United States. Some of them were willing to show-and I think my hon. friend from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) rather intimated the same thing-that all the advantage which England gets in the preferential trade is of an extremely flimsy description. I think some have put it as low as one-quarter or 1 per cent. I think the hon. gentleman admitted that it was one-third of 1 per cent. What particular figure they may finally settle upon is a matter for their own consideration, but I would point out to them, that if that consideration be a mere flimsy and trivial matter, if the preference is of very little importance, is it not rather an audacious request on their part and would it not be one on ours, to ask that the English people should, abandon their old and well-settled policy for so very trifling a consideration. I am not of the opinion myself that it is of such a trifling advantage. I think it is a matter, on more than sentimental grounds, of very considerable importance to the English manufacturer and exporter that whereas German and American competitors have to pay $3, he is only called on to pay $2, and I entirely differ from the hon. gentleman in thinking that the great consuming population of Canada fail to reap a large advantage from that reduction. Also-though I think they did not dwell much on that point - I have noticed that many of them complain that this reduction so trivial in consequence and insignificant in its character, has worked a great deal of injury to our own manufactures. There also I do not agree with



them, although I dare say some may be more or less inconvenienced by the fact that they have to compete on less favourable terms with England in our market.
Then these hon. gentlemen are constantly complaining of the extravagance of this government and constantly pointing to the fact that we are spending a great deal more money than they did-with which point I shall deal later on-yet almost in the same breath you will find these hon. gentlemen, or some of the leading men among them, constantly urging the government forward to new and heavy expenditure, in some cases expenditures, which, if carried out at all, would probably mean an addition of some hundreds of millions of dollars to our national debt. Sir, I would advise these hon. gentlemen to agree with each other-though perhaps that would be too hard, considering their traditions-and if they can agree with each other, I would advise them to formulate, and to formulate without much delay, some definite policy ; and, when they have so done, to challenge the policy of the government.
speakername: The MINISTER OF TRADE AND COMMERCE.

speechtext: And you would adopt the policy ?
As you did the national policy.

No, I think my hon. friend is speaking in considerable ignorance of the real effect of the introduction of the preferential tariff, and other changes made in the tariff of 1897. If he means to say that our tariff is a very high revenue tariff, I will agree with him ; if he says it is a protective tariff, I differ. And I will tell him that the best test of a protective tariff the world over is this-and he will see it exemplified on the other side of the border-that under a protective tariff imports go down. Under our tariff imports have expanded marvellously.
Now, it is inevitable, under the circumstances, that I must go over some of the old ground. If our friends on the other side will persist in making these unfair comparisons, if they will ignore the changed conditions of the country and the new services we have to provide for, if they will ignore entirely the proposals which they themselves made in 1896 from this side of the House, it becomes our duty, whenever they take that line, to remind them, and to remind the country, of what the real, actual position of affairs was. Now, in 1896, the then Finance Minister, Mr. Foster, brought down main estimates-and it was perfectly well known that he had very large supplemental estimates in reserve, though I will not go over that ground now- these main estimates alone showing that he required $38,358,000 for the services of 1897. We will start with his main estimates ; for the sake of the argument, I put on one side the well known fact that he Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
must have introduced, had his government remained in power, very heavy supplemental estimates in addition. These hon. gentlemen declare that we are enormously and atrociously extravagant, because my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), in the year last past, has expended $43,000,000, or nearly so. Now, I will admit that an additional expenditure of $4,600,000, in round numbers, is a very large addition to the annual expenditure ; it is a thing to be inquired into, a thing to be explained. But, before these hon. gentlemen declare that the mere fact that $4,600,000 more was spent in 1900 than was asked for in the main estimates alone for 1897 proves extravagance on our part, they will do well, and the House will do well, to consider under what circumstances this additional expenditure was required. I speak now, of course, of the sum chargeable to consolidated fund alone. I find that of the $4,600,000 additional expenditure, at least $1,500,000 was required for the services of the Intercolonial Railway, every penny of which was recouped to the treasury from the added receipts of the Intercolonial Railway. And a sum nearly as large was required for the service of the Yukon territory, for which the late government did not need to provide one farthing ; and this sum likewise was recouped the people of Canada out of the receipts of the Yukon territory. This service has not cost the people of the older provinces one single stiver. In fact. I am rather inclined to believe that the balance is the other way, and that we have a fair amount to our credit as a result of our expenditure on the Yukon. Then, about $500,000 was spent in the reduction of our debt in the added sum spent for sinking fund. If you want to make a fair comparison of expenditure, from this $4,-
600,000	you must take the $3,500,000 which appeared on both sides of the account. That is only common fair-play. And, when that is done you find that the alleged increase of $4,600,000 diminishes to a total increase at the end of the fourth year of $1,100,000-giving, as I said, the hon. gentlemen the benefit of the fact that I have simply taken their main estimates and have entirely left out of sight the enormous supplemental estimates that they would have had to bring down. Now, the total receipts from the railways and canals was, in 1896, $3,490,000, and, in 1900, $5,232,000. being an increase of receipts at the end of the fourth year of $1,638,000. Our expenditures for the same purpose, in 1896, were $3,826,000, and, in 1900, $5,244,000. So. our expenditures increased $1,418,000, while our receipts increased $1,638,000. I do not lose sight of the fact that there was considerable expenditure on capital account during that interval, but I point out that the interest on that account, up to June 30, 1900, was met, and, I believe, fully met, by the additional sum we received from the Intercolonial
Railway. Sir, I would like to ask kon. gentlemen opposite how muck tke poorer we were owing to tke fact tkat my kon. friend tke Minister of Railways now spends five millions or five and a quarter millions on tke Intercolonial Railway, and gets back five and a quarter millions ; kow muck poorer we are because we spend a million and a quarter or a million and a kalf in tke Yukon and receive a million and a quarter or a million and a kalf from tke Yukon ; kow muck poorer we are because we are debited on the one side with kalf a million of sinking fund and reduce the other side by purchasing kalf a million out of the sinking fund ?
There is another way of looking at this question tkat kon. gentlemen opposite would do well to consider. As I have said, tke conditions are mightily changed. In 1896, when these proposals tkat I alluded to were brought down, we had a very considerable deficit. We were threatened with a deficit in 1897. In 1895 our total available income, after providing for tke fixed charges-for interest and sinking fund, subsidies to provinces, and expenses known as ' collection of revenues '-was $7,000,000. In 1897. things were somewhat better; our total available income was about $10,000,000. In 1900, making these self-same deductions, our available income was about $21,000,000. That is to say, our available income is treble what it had been in 1895, and it is double our available income-which is the point which hon. gentlemen should chiefly consider in regard to these matters-of 1897. And, while our available income had increased over 100 per cent, our expenditure on the same basis-putting on one side the fixed charges and expenses known as ' collection or revenue,' which, as I said, are recouped-was about 10 per cent more than it had been in 1896 and 1897-the expenses of the two years not varying materially. Under the circumstances, it does not lie in the mouths of hon. gentlemen opposite to say that this government has been very reckless or extravagant In the additions it has made in public expenditure. And, if the House wants to know how the remaining $1,100,000, for which we are fairly accountable, is made up, I can give him in gross-I shall not inflict on hon. members the minute details-the three main items that have caused that increase. One of these was a considerable expenditure on the militia, to which I never heard a whisper of opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite. Another was a heavier expenditure on the part of my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) ; and, if I remember well, very few indeed of his items were challenged in detail.
The third large item was caused by my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture in the expenditures he made, with the unanimous approval of this House, for the purpose of developing and expanding our trade 48$	[DOT]
in agricultural products of various kinds ; the fourth was for the purpose of increasing and extending the immigration into this country on the part of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior. Now, Sir, if I am correctly advised, the result of my hon. friend's operations, in brief, has been this, that probably within the last three or four years-and here again he can correct me if I am in error-something like 30,000 or
40,000	farms have been taken up in Manitoba and the North-west, are now being brought into cultivation, and are adding largely to the resources, and wealth, and exporting power of this country. These were the objects for which we incurred an additional expenditure. Up to the present moment they have not been challenged by hon. gentlemen, and I doubt very much whether here or elsewhere hon. gentlemen will venture to challenge the expenditures incurred for these particular purposes ; and if they do not venture to challenge them, if they are content to allow them to pass with their entire approval, then I say we are perfectly justified in saying that the additional expenditure we have incurred is either, as I have already said, wholly and entirely in the nature of cross entries where, for every penny we spend we get a penny back, or that it is for purposes which command the unanimous approval of this House and of the people of this country.
But, Sir, perhaps it is when we turn to the developments of trade and commerce that we are able to see better than in almost any other way how great and how vast are the strides which this country has been making within the last four or five years. I spoke just now of the increased trade with the United States, and here it is worth while observing that this increase is to a certain extent a nominal increase. The nominal increase, I believe, was close upon $40,000,000 during the past year. But it is to be observed that we imported and exported, thus virtually neutralizing part of the item a much larger quantity of coin and bullion than in previous years, and it is also beyond doubt that a large part of our increased exports to the United States consisted of precious metals, which would find a market with perfect facility in any other part of the world, and as to which we cannot say that we are under much obliation to American customers for relieving us of them. Nevertheless, after making all allowances, there is no doubt that our trade with the United States has largely increased, and so far from holding that as any groupd for reproach, or any ground for misgiving, I for one am very glad indeed to know that our trade, and particularly our export trade with the United States, has incerased largely. A year or two ago our total export trade with the United States was about $45,000,000, our total export trade last year was $68,000,000, being
