There never was so good an advertisement given to any country, or to the productions of any country, as that given to the productions of Canada when we introduced preferential tariff. When hon. gentlemen say, as I think I heard one hon. gentleman say the other night, that not one man in a thousand in England knows anything or cares anything about the preferential tariff, I can tell him that there is probably not one man in a thousand in mercantile life in England who does not know and appreciate, and was not exceedingly impressed by the fact, that Canada alone of all the world had given a distinct preference to British goods in her markets. Sir, this is not a sentimental question. Great Britain stands in the position of a very rich and wealthy consumer who has the power of choosing between four or five rival competitors for her trade in goods nearly equal in quality, nearly equal in appearance. If you have the good-will of that customer you may rely upon it, and the people of Canada may rely upon it, that you will get a preference in the trade of that customer. In dealings with such a customer it is of great importance to have his good-will, and our people are finding it so more and more day after day. If our people will continue to send forward good articles, if they will avoid the danger which always besets trade when there is a rapid increase in the demand, of sending forward an inferior article, and relying on the previous excellence of their products to retain the market, I say if they will avoid that besetting sin, there is hardly any limit to the extent to which we may push our most profitable trade with England, more particularly as the articles which we have to sell are products of high quality, articles in which quality is looked to more than price by a very large portion of the English consumers with whom we deal.
Now, Sir, I do not see the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) in the House, but I would like to put a question or two to his confreres. If these hon. gentlemen complain that we have too great a surplus, if they allege, as I think I heard that hon. gentleman allege, that when you have a surplus it is your duty either to reduce the taxes or to reduce the debt, I would like very much to know from the opposition what particular taxes they propose to reduce. Sir, that is part of the express business of an opposition. If the opposition think that any taxes are oppressive on the people they have the fullest constitutional power to bring the question up here; and I for one, would be disposed to give most respectful consideration to any proposition that they may be pleased to advance for the reduction of taxes, whether it be on American goods, whether it be in the shape of a further extension of the British preference, or in any shape they please. There is a fair and full opportunity and I invite
them most cordially to do so, it they want to move to reduce taxation. They may also move to strike out Items of expenditure. It is fair, it is just and it is the duty of the opposition and I would he pleased, particularly In the matter of railway bonuses and other things of that kind, to see the opposition bestirring themselves actively In [DOT]the shape of reducing the various items which are brought down by the hon. Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and some other of my hon. friends. But, Mr. Speaker, I would say to hon. gentlemen opposite, that if they are not prepared to come forward and move for the reduction of taxation, if they are not prepared to strike out any special outlay, if they are not ready to abrogate the preference which we now grant to Great Britain, there is not very much object to be attained by prolonging the discussion of the budget brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding). It can serve very little good purpose for them or for us, to go over the old allegations which have been threshed out on every hustings in the Dominion of Canada during the last general election. There is one point, however, upon which I am disposed, and upon which my hon. friend beside me (Hon. Mr. Fielding) Is disposed, to partially agree with these hon. gentlemen. There is no doubt whatever that we have had a most extraordinary and .remarkable expansion of trade and commerce within the last few years, and I would be very sorry that this House, or this government should proceed to regulate their expenditure on the assumption that this will go on and continue until they had absolutely clear proof that the expansion was based on a permanent increase in production, which was perfectly sure to be maintained. However, on that head, I shall have a little to say before I sit down. I quite admit, as the history of Canada, of the United States, of Great Britain and of every other commercial country shows, that periods of great commercial expansion are apt to be followed by periods, either of depression, or of stagnation, and that a reasonable margin should be allowed to provide for such a case. Particularly, when the rate of increase has been as great and vast as it has been in our case, it would be folly for us to expect that it could be maintained ad infinitum. I believe I am speaking, for, not only myself, but, for my colleagues, also, when I say that we have fully realized that fact, that we have had it clearly before our eyes and that we design to regulate our future conduct in accordance therewith. But, Sir, in all these matters, after all said and done, there are two things which may be regarded as about the very best test of trade development in a country like this. One, I think, is the test of the great and rapid increase of trade and commerce; another is our -success in
filling up our waste lands and in adding largely to the active producers of this country. As regards the development of trade it is absolutely unparalleled ; the record is almost too good. The figures which my hon. friend beside me (Hon. Mr. Fielding) gave were sufficiently convincing, and if he erred at all, I think he erred on the side of moderation and hardly dwelt enough on the enormous rapidity with which our general trade, and more notably, our exports, have increased within the last few years. It is a very interesting fact that I now state to the House, that, within the last six months, the exports of our own produce, the produce of Canada amounted to $108,002,883. Before we came into office the exports for 1898-and it was a record year, it was the highest year that had been attained- amounted to $109,707,805. Six months of the present fiscal year equalled the highest record that up to that time had ever been attained in the fiscal history of Canada in the matter of the exports of our own produce. As to the total volume of our trade, I would like to call the attention of the House to this very notable fact, that, in 180S, the total volume of our trade was $131,027,532. In 1897, and it was a record year, it was the highest year we had ever attained, the total volume of our trade was $257,168,862. In these thirty years the total volume of our trade had increased by $126,141,330, and these were during the years in which we had added the whole of the Northwest Territories, the province of Manitoba, the province of British Columbia and the province of Prince Edward Island to our territory. Sir, in 1897, the total volume of our trade was, as I have already said, $257,168,862. In 1900, the total volume of our trade was $3S1,517,236, the difference being $124,348,374 in three years, as against $126,141,330 in thirty years. Sir, as to the question, and a very important question it is, whether the great growth in our exports is reasonably likely to be maintained, I have been at some pains to analyse the chief items of increase, and I am inclined to think, that, from the character and nature of the increases, there is a reasonable probability that the greater part, at any rate, of the expansion in our exports will be maintained, a point which all business men will regard as a very important matter. I find that our exports of bacon and hams in 1896 amounted to $4,381,968, while, in 1900, our exports of bacon and hams had grown to $12,758,025. In 1S96, our exports of butter amounted to $1,052,089, while, in 1900, our exports of butter totalled $5,122,563. In the matter of cheese our exports in 1896, were $13,956,571, while, in 1900, they were $19,856,324. In the case of the mines our exports in 1896, were $8,059,650, and in 1900, $24,580,266. Our exports in manufactures likewise increased very largely in these years. I would point out that these several items compose the major portion of the total

increases in our exports, and I think that there is reasonable ground to believe that these exports will not only be maintained, but probably will be increased with reasonable care and diligence on the part of our producers during the ensuing year or two. I need not say, Sir, that particularly in the case of the mines, these industries may be regarded as being almost in their infancy, that there is every ground in these and somewhat similar cases, as for instance, in the making of pulp, pulp wood, and paper therefrom, to look for a large and expanding trade. And now, Mr. Speaker, in concluding, let me ask if these facts be so, and I do not see how they can be successfully contradicted, is not my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) and are not the government fully justified in asking :	Why disturb so
prosperous a condition of things ; your trade is increasing, your debt is stationary, your population is increasing, your revenue is increasing, new resources are developing everywhere-why should we be asked to disturb so wholesome and goodly a condition of affairs ?
I doubt very much, Sir, whether these hon. gentlemen really believe that the existing condition of affairs could be bettered in any shape or form. I look around and 1 find it very difficult to ascertain where, if anywhere, there is any real discontent with the government. So far as I have been able to see, I am inclined to believe that the discontent which the hon. gentlemen opposite say exists may be confined to three classes. I am aware that there is a numerous class of gentlemen who are discontented with us because we have not made them senators. I am aware that there are certain manufacturers who are discontented with us because we have not chosen to allow the tariff to be used as an instrument for their private benefit; and I am aware also that the members of His Majesty's loyal opposition think, and, perhaps, with some reason, that we have had altogether too good times. I am inclined to think that that is beginning to dawn dimly upon their minds. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier), though he knew it not, had, to a certain extent, the spirit of prophecy on him when he almost predicted that we were here to stay, and to stay for five and twenty years. If that be so, I trust that my right hon. friend (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and his colleagues will be able, in these five and twenty years to administer the affairs of this country in such a way that when that time expires, they can point to equally as good a record as that we have the honour to submit to the consideration of the House and the country to-day.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure we have all listened with a great deal of pleasure to the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), but I dare say that some of us who were members of former Sir RICHARD CARTWRIGHT.
parliaments had our pleasure diminished by the fact that we had heard that same speech in various forms on several occasions of late years. I may remark that it differs very widely from the orations which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) was in the habit of delivering previous to 1896. I shall have occasion to make extracts from some of these former speeches of his, which will enable the House and the country to see what a wonderful distance the hon. gentleman has travelled, and how remarkable are his powers of locomotion. It would appear from what the minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) said at the eud of his speech, that no reasonable man could suggest the idea that a change is wanted in this country, but still he sits representing a province which has overwhelmingly condemned the administration of which he is a member. More than that, I am told that in the constituencies he visited as an active agent of the Liberal party, his presence produced most disastrous results.
Lincoln.

The county of Lincoln, with an assured Liberal majority of 600, was visited by the minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), and his visit was immediately fatal to the candidate of the Liberal party there. Wherever the hon. gentleman passed through Ontario, his trail was marked in all directions by dying and perishing victims belonging to the Liberal party. He visited Toronto, and that city is to-day, perhaps, the banner Conservative stronghold of all Canada. Now, the Minister of Trade and Commerce is apparently very anxious that the Conservative opposition should furnish the government with some variation of its present policy. I am not surprised at that, because any one who takes the budget speech and adds to it what has been said by the minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), will be inclined to remark that so far as power of initiating anything new is concerned, the government has shown an absolute want of efficiency. It has to-day a policy, and that remark may form a companion remark to the statement of the minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), that the opposition has no policy. Well, a man whose purse has been taken from him by a footpad has no purse, while the footpad has come into possession of one, and may vaunt it if he choose. The government to-day has a policy, but it is a policy which they appropriated from the opposition, and the government apparently glorying, the theft, twits the opposition with having no policy. I do not think, however, that it is the intention of the opposition to allow itself to be thus defrauded of its policy. Sir, the Conservative party of Canada stands to-day as it has stood for the last twenty-three years, prepared to maintain that policy of protection; the
policy of adequate protection. In that respect, I do not see that we could propound any policy that could be of advantage to our opponents, because notwithstanding the denial of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, they have shown themselves to be adepts, not in initiating a protective policy, but in the maintenance of a protectionist policy when it comes ready-made into then-hands. I was more struck by what the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not say than by what he did say, and particularly so, as he avoided, with the utmost care, any reference to that part of the speech of the member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), which most required attention at his hands. There can be no doubt that the belief exists in the lower provinces, whence I come, as well as elsewhere in Canada, that immediately previous to 1879, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) and his colleagues in the Mackenzie government, had, under pressure of public opinon, made up their minds to fall in with the views expressed in parliament by Sir John Macdonald and his lieutenants, in favour of protection to the manufacturing, the agricultural, the mining and the other interests. I have heard it told in detail that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) had prepared a protective tariff, when his purpose was interrupted by an incursion of free traders from the lower provinces, who threatened the Mackenzie government with the loss of their support unless the project was abandoned. It is told that then the hon. gentleman locked up in his desk his protective tariff, and he probably has it in the archives of his family to the present day. If that be not the ease, then it is difficult to attach any kind of meaning or relevancy to the remarks made by the premier at the banquet given .to the Minister of Trade and Commerce in April last, and in which the Prime Minister represented that hon. gentleman as showing great magnanimity and great loyalty to his party, in that he silently lay for eighteen years under the odium of having obstructed himself to the will of the people, and thus brought disaster upon his party, whereas, had he chosen to speak out, he could have shown that the fault did not lie with him. I regret that the minister (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) did not deal with that question, because the one thing which is altogether unsatisfactory about the budget speech is. that it leaves the government to-day standing in the equivocal position they have occupied since they came to power, of endeavouring to pose before the country as being in favour of protecting the manufacturers, and at the same time in favour of giving the consumers all they want. They are endeavouring to avoid the point at which it would be necessary to declare themselves, and to show whether they are protectionists or whether they are in favour of a revenue tariff-free traders, so called. The minister
(Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) told us last night, when he interrupted the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), that he was in favour of a revenue tariff which would impose a 20 per cent duty upon imports, and. that the condemnation to which he had been subjected was not because he refused to adopt a protective tariff, but because he refused to go beyond a 20 per cent tariff. The hon. gentleman declares that to-day he is in favour of a revenue tariff.
He maintains that he is to-day opposed to a protective tariff ; and still he sits as a member of a government which has at this moment not a maximum revenue tariff of 20 per cent imposed on all the importations of the country, but a tariff with duties as high as 5 cents a gallon on coal oil, 35 per cent on various lines of manufacture, and specific duties on every page. My hon. friend will not for one moment, I am sure, contend that the tariff which includes specific duties as high as 5 cents a gallon on coal oil, and which grants bounties to the extent of $3 a ton on pig iron, which the manufacturers tell us can be produced for something less than ?6 a ton, is in any sense a revenue tariff. Does the hon. gentleman ask the people of Canada to believe that he is sincere when he says that he is a strong upholder of a revenue tariff, while he sits in a government and draws the salary attaching to that government, which maintains a tariff such as I have described ? It is too much for human credulity. It is almost impossible to understand how the hon. gentleman can make s.uch statements in this House. However, that point has to a large extent been avoided. The hon. Minister of Finance has made no change whatever in the tariff, and so this matter goes for the moment over, and we are compelled-because in this House we must believe what is said by a member-to accept the statement that the tariff! of the government is a revenue tariff, although it imposes specific duties in all directions and grants bounties to the extent of 50 per cent of the cost of the materials produced, and imposes taxes on some commodities as high as 35 per cent, or even 50 per cent or 60 per cent, while it admits other commodities free of duty altogether, .in order that it may benefit and favour certain industries in the country. We have to believe, I say, in a technical sense, whatever is said in this House ; but I must say that the mental effort required to believe all these things is such a tax upon us that nothing but regard for an old statesman of Canada, a man who 'has grown gray in the service of the country, would induce us even to make the attempt to reconcile these hopeless discrepancies.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I was very much pleased yesterday to hear a budget speech of so very pleasing a character, both to the country and to the opposition-one of the most pleas-j ing that has ever been delivered In Canada ; because it is filled with good things-the

tidings of large revenues and abounding trade. I was pleased, during that discussion, to view the great delight which it afforded members sitting on the government side to feel that they were living in such a happy decade. Apparently, these gentlemen supposed that nothing of the kind had ever occurred before, and the Finance Minister, I believe, encouraged that belief in their minds. Now, it is always an unpleasant thing to dispel pleasing delusions. Still, we on this side of the House are always truthful; and I am compelled, out of regard for the truth, to give these gentlemen the knowledge which they might not seek for themselves, in the happy condition in which they live- that there have been kings before Agamemnon, that there have been surpluses in this country before the days of the present Liberal administration. In 1881, 1882, and 1S83, when Sir Leonard Tilley was Finance Minister of Canada, there were surpluses just as good, and I am compelled by truth to say even better than that with which the hon. Minister of Finance has met the House on this occasion. The surpluses of the Finance Minister which afforded such pleasure to his friends on the other side of the House, for the last three years amount to $14,615,000. For 1900, which is his banner year, he has a surplus of $8,054,000, a most amazing sum of money. Still, Sir Leonard Tilley, in 1883, had a surplus of $6,310,000, to which he added-and at that time my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) was sitting in the House, and did not contradict him, so that I presume a different system of book-keeping at that time prevailed-to which he added from the sale of Dominion lands $1,744,000, making a total surplus of $8,060,000, surpassing the boasted surplus of the present year by some $6,000. At present, I need scarcely say, receipts from the sale of Dominion lands' are to be found under the head of miscellaneous, and are included in the consolidated revenue of Canada. In 1884 Sir Leonard Tilley had again the pleasant duty devolving upon him of meeting parliament with a surplus of $7,064,492, and adding the receipts from the sale of Dominion lands amounting to $1,009,000, he was able to present to the House a total surplus of $8,073,492. And we must remember that that was 17 years in the past, when Canada was a comparatively small, poor, and unimportant country, compared with the Canada of to-day. At the same time Sir Leonard Tilley was in a postion to announce to parliament that the whole capital expenditure of the. country, amounting to $14,171,413, had been met in full without borrowing a cent of money outside of the revenues and the resources which came into the hands of the government. That achievement, I need scarcely say to my hon. friends who will take the trouble to recall the facts, eclipses the brilliant record which the Finance Minister was able to lay before parliament yesterday.

Another point that becomes interesting is to contrast the mode in which these different Finance Ministers dealt with this happy condition of affairs. We find that Sir Leonard Tilley showed a great desire to benefit the people of the country, and so managed the finances of that day that he reduced the net debt of Canada from $36.17 to $35.75 per head, and reduced the net interest on the debt of Canada from $1.64 to $1.50 per head, diminishing the annual impost on every individual in the country by 14 cents, or a relief of taxation on every family in the country of some 70 cents. Contrast that with the condition of things to-day. Does my hon. friend the Minister of Finance use his surplus, the golden harvest which has been gathered, for this purpose and in this way ? No. We find that under the present Finance Minister, who no doubt his friends on the other side of the House would like to suppose is a greater Finance Minister than has been, the debt has increased from $63.33 per head to $64.75, an increase of $1.42, and the net interest has increased from $1.74 per head to $1.78, an increase of 4 cents per head, showing a difference between the two of 18 cents as the result upon every individual in the country.
What was the condition of affairs in those years ? The capital expenditure of the government then was very high. It was the period just on the eve of the rebellion in the North-west, and when there was great activity in canal and railway building and tremendous demands on the treasury were being made. In those three years the capital expenditure of Canada was $29,729,000, or an average of $9,909,771 per year, whereas in the four years of the present administration. the capital expenditure has been only $23,358,000, or $5,839,000 per year. Contrast the two expenditures on capital account, that of this government, amounting to $5,-
839,000	per year, and that of the Conservative government, in the period I have referred to, amounting to $9,900,000 per year, and you will see how much less expenditure this administration has had to meet, and yet the ministers of the period I have referred to, when a Conservative administration held office, were able, despite the fact that our population and resources were smaller, to exhibit surpluses greater than even those of which this government boasts.
What is the contrast in another respect. It will be found that the Finance Minister has not distinguished his term of office since 1897 by any great reduction in the taxes of the people, if we except the 12} per cent, 25 per cent, and 33A per cent taken, under the preferential tariff, off the duties on British goods. With the exception [DOT] of this preference, the hon. gentleman has not made any reduction in the taxation. Compare his record in this respect with that of the late Sir Leonard Tilley. Sir Leonard Tilley in 1882 reduced taxation by one and a quarter million dollars, and in 1S83 by a like amount.
He took this amount off: the taxes 'with the full intention of diminishing the surplus and thereby lightening the burdens of the people, and yet, after making these reductions, he was still able to come before parliament with a surplus greater than that which the hon. the Finance Minister announced yesterday. It has been always held a proper policy for a finance minister to reduce taxation when he finds a buoyant revenue and a large surplus. I could recall capital speeches made by hon. gentlemen opposite-particularly by the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce, pointing-out the great danger attending a surplus and declaring that a finance minister, whose administration showed a large surplus, was not a good financial manager. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) has not succeeded in impressing this view, to which he so frequently gave such vigorous expression when in opposition, on his colleague, the Minister of Finance. The finance minister who succeeded Sir Leonard Tilley, the Hon. Geo. E. Foster, pursued the same course as did his predecessor. In 1891, when the country was very prosperous, when business was flourishing and the prospect of a surplus most certain, Mr. Foster took $2,000,000 off the taxes of the people, and he deliberately did so with the object of leaving that money in the pockets of the people instead of putting it into the treasury. He reduced the taxation of sugar by $3,500,000, and on the other hand imposed taxation of one million and a half dollars on malt, spirits and tobacco, making a net reduction of $2,000,000. But our present Finance Minister is wedded evidently to the opposite policy. His desire is to be able to boast of surpluses, but I do not know whether the people will enjoy his surpluses to the same extent as do the hon. gentleman and his supporters in this House. To my mind, the people would have far more reason to congratulate themselves if the Finance Minister would so manage the affairs of this country as to impose only such taxes as are necessary to avoid a deficit. But the hon. gentleman persists in keeping up the taxation'so that he may be able to boast of a surplus.
In 1878 the net debt of Canada was $124,-
551.000	; in 1896 it was $258,497,000, and in 1900 it was $265,000,000. There is nothing that seems to afford our hon. friends opposite so much pleasure as to make very unfair and misleading and improper statements in connection with the public accounts. During the few years they have been in office, they have had comparatively small capital expenditure to meet, compared with what the previous government had to meet in 1884 and 1885. The capital expenditure then rose to the point of $23,000,000 in one year. We then had to meet the cost of building the Canadian Pacific Railway and the expenses of the North-west rebellion, and were consequently adding to the
capital debt of the country at tho rate of $9,000,000 per year, as compared with a smaller capital expenditure of only $5,839,000 by this administration. So that it is not difficult to show that as regards the progress of Canada and the amount of money collected during the term of the present administration, and its addition to capital expenditure, that record is eclipsed by that of a previous Conservative administration.
I have indulged in these remarks principally because to a great extent the claim is made on the part of the government everywhere-not only on the hustings, but even here in the House of Commons, where men are supposed to know something of the facts -that we are living in an era of such prosperity as we never knew before, and that all this wonderful prosperity is entirely due to the financial guiding power and ability of our hon. friends opposite. This is a most absurd contention. I have pointed out facts to show that twenty years ago, when Canada1 was a poor country compared with today, a Conservative administration eclipsed the boasted record of the present government.
So far as the citizen of the country is concerned, he is not so much concerned in great surpluses as he is in economy. What is good for the citizen, ' the man in the street,' as he is called in the old country, is to have a government in power that will glvp him efficient service, security of life and property and light taxation. What is the record of this government in this respect ? They have not reduced 4axation, but have wonderfully increased it. It is true, they have, at various times in the past, condemned expenditures as extravagant and condemned them because they meant in- ' creased taxation. I might as well here recall to the memory of my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce who, I regret to see, has left his place, an utterance of his own when he was in opposition and criticising the administration, to show the position he occupied toward this matter of expenditure at that time. In criticising the budget speech of Hon. Mr. Foster in 1896- the last occasion when the task devolved on the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright)-he expressed himself in this way. And I may say to those who listened to his speech to-day and noted not only what he said, but made correct and careful note of what he did not say, that the remarks that I am about to cite offer a remarkable contrast with his utterance of to-day :
For my own part I do not hesitate to tell him that I consider a yearly expenditure of $40,000,000 of $38,300,000 altogether too large for the present resources of Canada. I say It is a disgrace and a shame to the government that have been entrusted with our affairs that they come down to us and ask for an expenditure of $38,300,000 a year for Federal purposes. Sir, the
thing is wholly unjustifiable	The
fact of the matter is that hon. gentlemen opposite have been discounting the future at a most

tremendous rate, and now the bills have come back and there are no assets wherewith to meet them. Sir, there is very little use on the part of hon. gentlemen whining over this matter. They ought to try and meet it, and the way to meet it is to reduce our present establishment, the way to meet it is to reduce your present extravagant mode of government and to reduce your extravagant ideas.
In 1897, the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Rickard Cartwright) went into power in company with his colleagues. In the year that had elapsed from the making of his speech in 1896 to his accepting office in 1897, affairs in Canada had changed only in that the recovery which was manifest in 1896 had continued to make its way. There was nothing in the circumstances of 1896 to justify the hon. gentleman In the statements he made, for instance, that we had been discounting the future at the most tremendous rate. We had been recuperating, we had been passing through a'period of hard times, a period of rest, a period when the country was economizing and had gained a position from which it could go forward to greater expenditure, could begin to live upon a higher and more extravagant scale-as is the habit of governments as well of private individuals. If these remarks had been made by the hon. gentleman today in criticising the budget speech of his hon. friend the Minister of Finance, they would have been proper. We have been discounting the future; we have been taking every dollar we could from these fat years and spending it; we have not been putting one dollar of it away to meet the lean years that are to come. These remarks of the hon. gentleman would have been pregnant,
. pertinent, wise, if they had been made in criticising the budget speech of to-day; they were neither wise nor applicable in criticising the budget speech of Mr. Foster in 1896. What is the reason the hon. gentleman, who was so critical then, who was so rabid that his judgment persuaded him to say what he knows he could not defend anywhere, to make statements that are contrary to the facts and not to be defended-what is the reason that the hon. gentleman, who was so prone to criticism then that he was led to be unfair and unjust, who criticised so severly an expenditure of $38,000,000, sees nothing wrong in an expenditure that will touch if it does not exceed $46,000,000 ? The sole change apparent to me and to the country is that the hon. gentleman himself has got into office. The course which he recommended to the Conservative administration of reducing our present establishment, reducing the number of ministers and the cost of government has not been carried out. The ministers have been increased in number, and among the gentlemen so added to what he called an unnecessarily large establishment is the hon. minister himself. The hon. gentleman, so long as he is in this House, will not get up and argue that he should not be here-I presume that he is Mr. BELL (Pictou).
too logical for that. Before he makes up his mind to criticise the administration, his resignation will reach the premier, and he will be able to make that criticism a candid one. Is it possible that he will hesitate to make that small sacrifice in order that he may become once more the keen, unspairing critic of extravagant administration in Canada ?
He could not do justice to it.

An hon. gentleman on this side has anticipated me. I am sorry that he who made so much of small opportunities during the years of Conservative administration is not on this side today. There is only one thing that would put him at a disadvantage-a lack of adjectives, I think he has quite exhausted the vocabulary in criticizing the Conservative administration. With such a task as would be presented to him if he were on this side, he would be in the position of the gentleman, who on one occasion was expected to indulge in a great burst of profanity, but said not a word except, ' I won't swear ; can't do justice to the subject.' Now, while we would like very much if we could have had the opportunity in indulging in an analysis of the fiscal management of this government, we would like also to lock horns with them on the subject of free trade or protection. We would like to have driven them out of the lines of Torres Vedras in which they are now so comfortably ensconsced, get them in the open and make them declare whether they are or are not in favour of protection. There is one subject on which our hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has given us a large invitation. He has asked us to name those expenditures we would like to have stopped, to specify the taxes we would like to have reduced. I think it is not very difficult to meet his views in that respect.
I think it would not be difficult, in the matter of public works, to make large economies without impairing the efficiency of the service. For instance, the expenditure on the Sorel bridge, to which attention has been called by the Auditor General, might have been much less without injury to any public interest. I think that numerous cases in which contracts are let without tender might have been managed by hon. gentlemen on this side so as to economize considerably.
I think we could have built telegraph lines in British Columbia without such expense as has been indulged in by these hon. gentlemen. I think we could have economized to the extent of a couple of millions in the subsidies to the Crow's Nest Pass Railway.
I think, on the other hand, if we had been on that side of the House during the last four years we could have been able to specify some matters in respect of which we would have removed the taxation. I
do not see why the Minister of Finance did not make some suggestions of that nature, while maintaining that protection of the industries, of this country in which we support him, and for which we give him credit, according us that sincerest form of flattery which he has administered to our vanity in imitating our policy. If we had been on that side of the House we could have suggested changes in the tariff which would have impaired the rotundity of his remarkable surplus, and which would not have impaired the rotundity of the purse of the public. We could have suggested the removal of the taxation on sugar, of the taxation on tobacco; we could have suggested that in many other respects which are properly the subjects of a revenue tariff, the tariff could have been reduced on the necessaries of life to the lowest possible point. But the hon. gentleman will probably not take our advice in this matter.
I do not think the hon. gentleman would'give it.

I am giving it in all sincerity. A government which is going to maintain a protective system can derive money enough from the duties on protected articles, and still relieve many other articles by making them subject to a revenue tariff.
Now, there is another point in reference to which the Minister of Finance seemed to be in a somewhat combative mood, he was very anxious to .have his course challenged in respect to the preferential tariff, he wishes that the opposition should challenge his course in that matter. The hon. gentleman reminds me of the miserable plight in which Sinbad the sailor found himself after he had foolishly allowed the old man of the seas to get upon his shoulder. He found himself choked and incommoded by the manner in which the old man of the sea gripped him about the neck, and when he suggested that the old man get off his shoulders, he, feeling very comfortable where he was, resigned to his situation, declined to quit. I believe the Minister of Finance with his preference to England on his back is in a similar situation, he put it there and let him keep it there. He is anxious apparently that the opposition should help him out of his dilemma. He blundered into it, he may blunder out of it; if not, let him blunder along until he falls under the weight of it, as he undoubtedly will. There can be no question whatever that if nothing else drives this government into a corner where they will be compelled to make an honest and public declaration of their policy, and to say whether they are genuine protectionists or hybrid free traders, it will be the operations of this precious preference to England. It is a thing that no man on
this side of the House approves. But, as I have said, our hon. friends have got themselves into this plight, and by all means let them stay there until they find some way of relieving themselves. Now, the objections to such a policy are numerous. In the first place, while there may be some value in the sentimental considerations which are asserted continually, they are very intangible. When the Minister of Trade and Commerce, with his great experience, spoke, I hoped to hear something important from him. When he told us today that he was prepared to defend the preference and challenged the opposition to say anything against it, I hoped to hear him say something to justify it. Now, what was the extent of his justification ? It was a bare assertion that the sentiment aroused, the effect produced upon the English mind by the knowledge of the fact that Canada alone of all the world had given that country a tariff preference, increased our exports to that country. The hon. gentleman made that assertion, I presume it was necessary for him to make some assertion, but did he furnish one vestige of proof of that assertion ? Did he suggest one consideration that made that assertion a probability, that made it a likelihood ? Not one. There is only the bald assertion that the kindly sentiments aroused in the minds of the English people by the preference we had given them, the fact that we had shown them a disposition to help them in the work of developing their trade, has earned for us a kindly place in their minds, to such an extent that they will buy our goods. Now, I do not believe that. I am prepared to believe it on reasonable proof, I have never heard any proof whatever, and I decline to accept even the assertion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that the one thing follows the other. The facts are against it. The relative developments of trade as proved by the figures cited last night by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) discredit the statement. The showing is that while our trade with Great Britain has increased, it has increased much more largely with other countries to which we have shown no favour whatever. The evidence goes to show that while our trade has increased with Great Britain, it has increased far more with the United States. So that the whole argument falls to the ground, and in calling it an argument, I am showing sincere kindness towards the Minister of Trade and Commerce, I am conceding to him a great deal out of a sense of politeness. To my mind it is an argument that does not carry conviction. On the other hand, this mode of assisting the British manufacturer is, to my mind, exceedingly objectionable. What is the fact of the case ? Supposing that we wanted to benefit England, supposing we wanted to bestow a large advantage upon

her, the greatest advantage we can possibly bestow on her is by maintaining a good understanding with that country, by drawing closer and closer the ties of kinship and the feeling of kindness, while at the same time endeavouring to build up this country to a point, to a stature, at which it will be a more and more powerful ally and a strong arm to Great Britain, if she should ever need our help.
Now, how can we do that ? That question was settled in 1879. One of the objections made at that time to the establishment of a protective tariff in Canada was that it was an unfriendly act towards Great Britain, a country which depended upon its manufactures, which prized its foreign trade. It was argued then that possibly the British government might even disallow our protective tariff on the ground that it was striking at British trade. But the men of that day who passed the national policy, who put the national policy into operation, had considered all these things, they met the objection that it was an unfriendly act to Great Britain, they faced that bugbear, for bugbear it was, they were not frightened by it, and they faced that consideration in 1879, and settled it then. Their protective tariff was not hampered, or impaired, or emasculated, by sentimental consideration for the manufacturers of Great Britain. Nothing of the kind was allowed to affect the efficiency of the national policy at that time, and nothing of the kind should be allowed to affect the efficiency of the national policy to-day. Therefore, I say if this administration is ever brought to their knees, when pressure of hard times will come to the manufacturing industries of this country, and bring them to that point where they will approach the government for relief, if this government is then going to maintain the position of a protectionist administration, it will have to look carefully into the effect of this preferential tariff. I believe that the very preference into which this administration fell by accident will force them at a very early date to declare themselves either straight protectionists, as I would like to see them, or to go back to their old love which was inculcated in them by Brown, Mackenzie and all the other worthies who were leaders of their party before 1879, and to declare themselves a free trade or a revenue tariff party, not only so, but to live such a life in the eyes of men as will prove them to be a free trade and a revenue tariff party.
Now, what is the objection to this preference ? It is sometimes called a concession made to the British public. If it is a concession it amounts to very little. It is one that is conferred not upon the whole British population, but only upon a section of it. Now, the whole effect of the preference so far has been to increase the im-

ports of Canada from Great Britain in the last year by $7,729,000.
Now, as this is rather an important point, perhaps I had better deal with it as a whole. The total imports of Canada in 1896 were $110,000,000, and in 1900, $189,000,000. Our total trade in imports increased in four years $79,000,000. The increase in the last year, this extraordinary year, this year in which we have had a most startling development of trade, has been $35,000,000, or nearly $30,000,000. Great Britain's part of this business, for the year 1896, amounted to $33,000,000, and for the year 1900, to $45,000,000. In exact figures, our trade with Great Britain increased in four years by $11,809,988, and in the last year, in which the most satisfactory increase has been made, satisfactory from the point of view of those who like that kind of thing, because it has been very well said that for people who like that kind of thing, that is the kind of thing they like, the increase was $7,729,G07. We, on this side of the House, do irot like it at all, because, as far as we can see. this increase lias been at the expense, not of the whole people of Canada, but at the expense of a very limited class of the people of Canada, a matter to which I will refer later on. Taking now the United States imports, they amounted to $58,000,000 in 1896, while, in 1900, they amounted to $110,000,000. showing an increase in four years of $51,000,000, and in the last year, an increase of $17,000,000. Relatively, the increase in trade from Great Britain is larger. It is not surprising that it should be so, but the whole increase in our trade from the United States, amounting to $17,000,000, is more than double the increase in trade from Great Britain. Our imports from other countries also increased. We bought, in 1896, $19,000,000 worth, and in 1900. $35,000,000 worth. In four years our trade with other countries increased by nearly $16,000,000. and in the last year it increased by $9,000,000, so that, as compared with the rate of increase in our trade from Great Britain, it does not show to advantage at all. Our trade from a number of other countries increased from $19,000,000 to $35,000,000, and in the last year it increased by $9,000,000, whereas the trade from Great Britain showed an increase of $7,729,007 last year. However, this is not as conclusive, perhaps, as the figures given by the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy), because, he showed that, whereas the government party are, in this matter, driven to argue and to try and persuade the public that we are getting our advantage indirectly, that while we are increasing our imports from Great Britain, to a great extent, we are largely increasing the exports from this country, his evidence goes to show that Great Britain stood eighth in tile list of countries in the order or proportion of their trade. So that, the fact of the
matter is, that despite this preference given to Great Britain, our trade with that country has not increased as rapidly as it has with other countries to which we make no concession whatever.
Now, there is another very marked objection to this preference. It is given only to a special class in Great Britain. It is given only to a very limited portion of that class, because there are very many lines of manufacture in Great Britain which cannot compete with similar industries in the United States or in Canada. The advantage therefrom is derived by the manufacturers of woollens and some lines of metal. In wood, tobacco, and other manufactures they cannot compete. We can hold our own in manufactures of paper, and some other lines, and the consequence is that the scapegoat, the man who is called upon to make all these sacrifices in order that Canada shall acquire certain advantages of a sentimental character, is the manufacturer of a comparatively limited number of lines of goods in Canada. Take the manufacturers of woollens, for instance ; they tell us that they cannot face the competition to which they are subjected under a tariff that has been reduced by 33* per cent. Why should a certain industry be singled out for destruction in order to secure a sentimental consideration of this kind ? If Canada wishes to confer an advantage on the empire, it should put a tax on all the citizens of Canada to defray the cost of that advantage, and not throw this burden upon one particular class. Apart from that, no man who is thoroughly in favour of adopting protection as the national fiscal system of Canada can justify that process, if it be one that throws a burden upon any particular industry in the country. The whole purpose of protection is to protect ; and to introduce into the system a provision which makes it inefficient is a coui'se that can be followed by no government that honestly believes in protection. For a protective government to have tacked to this system such a form of modifying the tariff as this preference, is to show that these hon. gentlemen do not understand what they are doing, when they are, on the one hand, protecting by their system some industries, and on the other excluding some industries from its advantages. If, at the same time, their system is allowed to go to its legitimate end, it must end in disaster to the whole system, to the industries of the country, and they will be forced to deal with the subject at an early day.
There were a great many things in the budget speech which were very pleasing, because they conveyed to us the knowledge that the country is prosperous. However, there were a good many things not dealt with that one would naturally expect to be contained in a message indicating the condition of prosperity in which the country is. There are, I think, many portions of the
world to which we might turn our eyes with the view of extending our trade. In the last budget speech, one of the most notable points was the information as to a proposed arrangement with a portion of the West Indies, by which we expected to develop a certain amount of trade in that direction. Unfortunately, that matter fell through, and it is a somewhat singular thing that, in the budget speech made this year, there is no reference whatever to any negotiations, or any attempt to regulate, or improve our relations with outside countries, and notably, no intimation made whatever to show that any effort has been made to develop our trade with the West Indies. This is a matter in respect to which I think the government should be alive ; they should be awake and hard at work. I believe it is only necessary for Canada to take in the West Indies to round out her confederation, to make it a perfect government, to give it all those diversities of climate, soil and product that will make it a selfsupporting and practically independent part of the world. With the addition of the West Indian islands, so far as this country is concerned, I would not exchange places with the United States, powerful as they are. I think in that case we will be a microcosm, a little world, and we will have added to our territories a contiguous territory which would enable us to develop some very valuable resources. Then, there is another point, and that arises in- connection with the preference tariff, to which I have paid some little attention. That is, the discrimination of Germany against the products of Canada. The government makes no reference to that. Apparently the government has never thought of it. Is the government prepared to take any action now to protect Canadian interests or is it inert ? Is it aware of this fact, or is it in the position of the Minister of Railways, who discovered only from a private telegram read by a private member, that an important portion of his railway system was blocked up by snow ? Is it possible that the administration is not aware that discrimination is being used against the exports of this country in Germany ? Is it possible the government has no remedy tn offer ? Is it not a singular thing that in the one opportunity during the year which the Finance Minister has of telling the people of Canada how he is looking after their affairs and what proposals he has to make for the future, that the Finance Minister neglects to give any consideration to a most important matter affecting the country ? Or is it possible that the government shrink from their duty ? If so, I would remind them that here again there is a contrast between their attitude and that of the Conservative administration, because so far back as 1883 Sir Leonard Tilley said :
If we fail to make satisfactory arrangements with the governments that do not place the

natural products and the manufactures of Canada on equal terms with those of any other country, we will ask parliament, at the next session, to impose a duty of 10 per cent additional on their products until they grant us such terms.
That is what we are doing now.
Where ?
That is exactly what we are doing now ; imposing a material difference-not exactly 10 per cent-between the duties on German goods and British goods.
That is a most unworthy statement.
It happens to be a fact, and I suppose therefore the hon. gentleman thinks it unworthy.
It just shows the size of the calibre that suits the Finance Minister.
The House can judge of calibre between us.

It is just about his size. What he does is actually to put Germany on an inequality with one other country in the world and leaving her exactly equal with every other country in the world. That is a most unworthy statement of the Finance Minister, and I would be tempted to use even the stronger word ' evasion' in reference to the unfortunate remark made by the hon. gentleman.
I do not happen to think so ; we will have to differ.

I do not doubt at all the difference would be in my favour. Then we are to assume that the duty apparently has been discharged by the government. We now have it on the 'high authority of the Finance Minister that they have dealt with this question, and, therefore, I presume I need not waste my time in arguing further on the question.
Hear, hear.

We know from the Finance Minister that they have, done all that is necessary under the circumstances. They are apparently satisfied. Germany can go on and discriminate against Canada and I presume the government will still impose that 10 per cent-as the Minister of Finance says-discrimination against her in the same vigorous and effective manner in which they are imposing it now. Hurrah for this government. It is a great day for Canada that its interests are so well guarded.
My hon. friend had better explain what he would do about it.

I have already explained what a predecessor of this Finance Mr. BELL (Pictou).
Minister would do about it, and although I am not in a position to promise too much, I venture to assure the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that so far as he does at any time stand up and strike a blow in the interest of Canada as against any foreign country, he will have the support of the Conservative opposition of this House.
Now, Mr. Speaker, 1 have gone, somewhat inadequately perhaps, over the various features of the budget speech that attracted my attention. I regret very much to find that the charge which has been made at times against this administration, not only by members of the opposition but by the independent people of the country, is borne out by the facts as we see them, to-day. The great merit of this administration since 1897 was in their capacity to follow. Their great good fortune was that they succeeded an administration which lived a long time and which gave that feature of stability and firmness to the tariff which the Finance Minister (Hon. Mr. Fielding) spoke of as a good thing that attracted his commendation and approval. But, Sir, that quality of stability and permanency in the fiscal system of Canada has not altogether grown up during the years which the hon. gentleman has been Finance Minister. It has been a characteristic of that system since 1879, and that these last four years have not been an unfortunate exception to that stability is due to the fact that he and his friends very properly determined', to follow in the footsteps of their predecessors and in consequence to abandon every profession and every pledge they made while in opposition. In every department of government these gentlemen in office have acted most wisely in continuing the course of their predecessors. They have disturbed nothing. In connection with this, perhaps I may read an extract from the speech of the Minister of Finance in 1897, when he found it necessary to turn that sharp corner which they had to take. He said :
Every man who invested a dollar in the national policy

That is, I suppose, in the industries fostered by the national policy, because I do not think this was a policy game, although it had a policy name.
Every man who invested a dollar in the national policy did so with his eyes wide open to certain important facts. He was well aware that from the beginning down to the end the national policy was condemned by one of the great political parties in Canada.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wonder what party that was.
You will find out by-and-by.
It will be in the sweet by-and-by when we pass from this sublunary sphere. I think it has gone to that limbo in which ghosts and disembodied spirits play their part.
I will be able to tell you one hon. member who condemned It.
How does lie vote now ?
He is on the opposite side of the House.
He probably is and votes for this revenue tariff-protective administration.
And bounties on iron.

And bounties on iron, no doubt. I go on with the reading of the extract :
He was well aware that every effort had to be put forth by governmental influence and such influences as the manufacturers themselves are well aware of

I wonder if the manufacturers are well aware of these influences now. I have reason to think that during the last campaign in the country the manufacturers were well aware of these Influences and were looked to by the government to exert themselves.
More so than ever.

Even to a greater degree perhaps. I quote again :
*-in order to obtain from the public an apparent endorsement of that policy.
Apparently that endorsement was satisfactory because it has passed current with the gentlemen who came into power; it was discounted in full.
Now, the manufacturers knew of this and they must have known that when they put their money into these factories they were taking their risks. There was a speculative element in the whole national policy business, and the men who played the game and gathered in the winnings ought to be prepared when the turn of the tide comes, to pay the losses and try to look pleasant.
I am surprised to find that my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Melding) speaks so familiarly in the language of a certain element of sports in which I did not know he was so well versed.
He probably visited New Glasgow occasionally.

I quote again from the Finance Minister :
I wish to emphasize the fact that it never has been the policy of the Liberal party, as declared by any member of the Liberal party occupying a responsible position, if they came into power to destroy at one movement all the manufacturing industries or so change that policy as to place them in peril.
What a lovely thing it was that all the time these gentlemen were going about Canada denouncing protection and the bloated monopolists, and the thieves, and robbers, and praying no doubt night and morning for the salvation of that unhappy victim who had been bled white-is it not a lovely
thing to know that during all that time these hon. gentlemen were carrying in their breasts this lovely reservation ; this saving grace, this clause that saved them ; that it was never their idea when they came into power to destroy by one fell movement the policy of protection. And here I take it there is another saving clause apparently. They are not to destroy it by one movement, but they are to destroy it by a very great number of small movements, and by a graduation so imperceptible that we will not get to the end of it when that period of 25 years has expired which we have been talking about. The Finance Minister goes on to say :
We denounce the principle of protection as radically unsound and unjust to the masses of the people. And we declare our conviction that any tariff changes, based on that principle, must fail to afford any substantial relief from the burdens under which the country suffers.
That issue we unhesitatingly accept, and upon it we await with the fullest confidence the verdict of the electors of Canada.
What issue was that ? It was the issue of a gentleman who believed in free trade, who denounced protection, but who, with his healthy and wholesome reservation, thought that his creeds, his convictions, did not pledge him at all to destroy the manufacturing industries of the country or place them in peril, or change the policy that existed. That is the issue-a lovely issue, a double-barrelled issue; an issue which placed him not between the two horns of a dilemma, but between two comfortable seats on either of which he might reach office. The Finance Minister calls that an issue. Yes, it is a very satisfactory one for him and his party; they are in power, the industries of the country have not been interfered with, and the policy has not been disturbed. I do not know that he will find any party in this country ready to grapple with him on that issue, unless possibly some third party arises that would be willing to do so. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) might be prepared to take up that issue; but as long as we are limited in this country to the two great issues of a revenue tariff on the one hand and protection on the other, it will be difficult to find a party ready to join issue with a party which believes in both of these things, at once.
Now, a great feature of my hon. friend the Finance Minister's policy when he was in the government of Nova Scotia was to do nothing-to draw his salary and stay in office; and possibly his coming to this government marks the adoption of such a policy here. We will see whether this system, which worked so well in a small field, will be equally successful in the larger one, and whether this government will succeed simply by staying in office and drawing their salaries. While I am prepared to look as favourably on this government as any man in Canada who is an opponent of theirs, I

do begin to fear that there is a little truth in the criticism which has been directed against them, that they lack initiative. What have they done or originated since they came into power in 1890 1 What have they changed ? Well, they changed one thing: I believe they turned down the fast Atlantic service, and they have not yet revived it. I have no doubt, however, that true to their system of sooner or later carrying out those features of their opponents' policy which they come to believe are popular with the public, they will ultimately revive that project. But what have they themselves initiated ? What new departure have they made ? I ask for an answer, and there is no answer. Nothing; they have made no change; they have shown no originality, no inventiveness, no ingenuity. I believe their whole idea is to do just as my hon. friend the Finance Minister did when he was in the government of Nova Scotia-avoid running up against anybody's prejudices or doing anything that would provoke opposition, but hang on to the sweets of office as long as possible.
There is one great party in Canada which has never been known to be satisfied with simply doing nothing. The Conservative party had its faults, no doubt, because no man or party is faultless; but it was a party which had thrown upon it the burden of developing a great country, and they developed it. They had to take upon themselves that task at a time when this country was comparatively poor, a task which might have daunted the legislators of a much older and richer country, and they performed that task, I need scarcely say, in the face of a great deal of opposition from hon. gentlemen opposite. They wrought out everything of value which we have in Canada to-day-our system of government, our canal system, our railway system, our judicial system. Everything of value which we have in Canada to-day was set in motion by the Conservatives. There is not a single thing in Canada to-day, except that preference into which these gentlemen fell or blundered, to show that they are in power, except the fact that they are drawing their salaries and occupying their offices and that their names appear attached to certain public documents. Now, there is work for them to do. There is a tremendous task lying immediately in front of the government of Canada, and that is to go on and develop and jJerfect that system of international preference which we who are Imperialists long to see and under which this country will grow up as one of a great band of sister nations associated with the mother country. We want to see the trade between the mother country and all the colonies developed. The Finance Minister says it cannot be done- you cannot get this preferential trade. Why not ? He says you cannot get it because Lord Salisbury is not in favour of it, because Mr. Chamberlain is not in favour of it; and

he rests his opinion of Mr. Chamberlain's views on a newspaper article which referred to what occurred in an informal interview which a gentleman of Ottawa had with Mr. Chamberlain. But are we to cease exerting ourselves to secure this great and desirable result simply because certain statesmen of the mother country express themselves unfavourably to it ? No. That was not the course pursued by the Conservative government. Hon. gentlemen know what obstacles the Belgian and German treaties were in the way of preferential trade, and how the government of Canada for twenty years asked that those obstacles should be removed, and were met with a constant refusal. They know how, when the colonial convention met in Ottawa, a formal request was made for their removal, and how that was refused also. Then, hon. gentlemen opposite had the good luck to come to the day of reaping after all that sowing, and in their time these treaties, which we were told could not be abrogated, were denounced by the British government. These gentlemen, by their preferential tariff, blundered into such a position that it forced the hand of the mother country

Hear, hear.
Mr. BELL (Pictou)-and the mother country, in kindness, to help them out of their difficulty-because at that time the preference, instead of being a preference to Great Britain, was extended, through the blundering of these gentlemen, to no less than twenty-three countries. Laugh now, if you please. I think there are quite a number of new members in this House, Mr. Speaker, who laugh a little out of place. The preference was extended to twenty-three countries, not one of which had extended corresponding benefits to this country which were supposed to be necessary in order to get the preference. Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that it was not a blunder that compelled him and his government to admit the goods of all these countries into this country under the preference, while they maintained hostile tariffs against us ? One happy result was the abrogation of the German and Belgian treaties by the British government, and the result of that abrogation shows that the Conservative contention that Great Britain would not suffer was the correct one. Both Germany and Belgium were willing to renew the treaties without the objectionable feature.
Let these hon. gentlemen make another move and see whether they cannot blunder into another such situation. They may not do it by design, but may by accident, but if they do not move at all, whatever chance we might have of taking advantage of the present opportune moment may be lost. Theirs is a great work to be accomplished, and that work will not be done if these hon. gentlemen will restrict themselves to considering simply what Lord Salisbury or
Mr. Chamberlain wants or even what the people of England want. We are rapidly attaining the position in this world in which our sister colonies and ourselves stand on a position of equality, so far as wealth, industry and energy are concerned, with the people of the mother country, and I should not be at all surprised if it would be the happy function of my right hon. friend and those associated with him to show the way to the statesmen of Great Britain of accomplishing a policy which will make all parts of this great empire one in selfinterest as well as in sentiment. We have solved problems in Canada that might well have daunted the statesmen of any country. We have, in the course of a few years, with a handful of people, created a great empire without any help from Downing Street. We have shown what a comparatively small people can accomplish. Then let these hon. gentlemen on the government benches not be discouraged by a simple refusal to be heard in Downing Street, let them leave Downing Street severely alone, and approach the people of Australia and the other British colonies in different parts of the world, and let all these branches of the one great family make common cause and approach unitedly the British government. I have given my right hon. friend credit for more ability than he thinks he possesses, for I believe that with the assistance of the premiers of the other colonies he would be able to formulate a scheme by which the mother country and all her colonies could enter into the full enjoyment of a common preferential tariff. The task lies at the hands of this government, and I hope that when we next meet, the government will be in a position to show the people of Canada that they are in sympathy with the great mass of our people, because our people do believe in the advantage of preferential trade and a fiscal system that would knit into one whole all the English-speaking colonies. I hope that the government will show themselves alive to the necessities of the hour, and will come here next session, if not with a complete scheme, at least with the facts collected which will enable the people to arrive at some conclusion as to the best method of accomplishing what the great majority desire.
I am sorry that it has been my painful duty to tear away that vision of golden enjoyment in which the Prime Minister and his supporters are now revelling. It is too bad that I should have been able to show that when this country was not half as rich as it now is, it could boast of as large surpluses and show a much better use made of the money, and at the same time show a considerable reduction in taxes.
I congratulate my hon. friends on the fact that they are living in such good times. I also congratulate my hon. friend the Mln-49
ister of Finance on the fact that he has not lost the shrewdness for which he was noted in our province. Like an experienced sailor, he is evidently quite aware that a gale is brewing. He sees the skies darkening, the waters foaming, and is taking in a reef and preparing the crew for rough weather before long, so that they may not be too much disturbed when the winds break on the vessel and the salt seas flow over it. But the hon. gentleman's views have changed considerably. When he was in opposition, and a reaction set in, anti the tide of prosperity changed, he and his friends said that was a proof of misgov-ernment, that the country was, being robbed and everything going to the dogs.
On this side of the House, however, we do not take that position. We are prepared to admit that it is perfectly natural the tide should turn, and are pleased that the Finance Minister should see the change coming, but we would be better pleased if we saw some preparation for the change in the estimates. No doubt, however, this administration finds it hard to make the expenditure any smaller than that in which they have been indulging during the last four or five years.
The hon. gentleman speaks of this approaching period of depression, not as the result of misgovernment-as he would have done were he in opposition-but as a necessary period of rest and recuperation, and upon the existence of which he is actually in a position to congratulate the country. Why, it is almost worth the money it has cost Canada to see how these gentlemen have changed their views. Depression is no longer an evidence that the country is being mismanaged and misgoverned, but is merely an evidence that the country is resuming a more healthy condition and getting ready for greater exertions in the future. How is it that that view of the question never struck that wonderfully wise man the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) during eighteen years? It may have struck him, he may have been fully impressed with it, but if so he kept his opinion profoundly secret. When on this side, he was always prepared to denounce and never to praise, but things have wonderfully changed since the hon. gentleman obtained office, and to-day we have him admitting what he would have never acknowledged previous to 1896, namely, that Canada is getting rich.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance pointed to the deposits in the post office savings bank, and to the note circulation as evidences of prosperity. Well, I have been pretty observant in political affairs, and I never met during the years the late government was in power any Liberal speaker who was prepared to admit that there was anything in such matters. They would all tell us that undoubtedly the country was being bled white for the benefit



of the bloated manufacturers and that the deposits in the savings banks and the note circulation did not mean anything. It is really gratifying to find these hon. gentlemen converted to more rational views.
But, I fear that my hon. friend the* Finance Minister may not have anticipated the full force of the approaching gales. He is still figuring on a very large surplus. I hope he may get it, but there are certain indications that the stringency coming may be more severe than the hon. gentleman anticipates. There are certain things which indicate the coming change. The hon. gentleman spoke of the wonderful development of our exports. Well, I have not the advantage of access to the latest documents as has the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I have access to the customs returns to the end of November, and I find that while the exports of bullion from the Yukon amounted to $14,000,000 or $15,000,000 over the same five months of the preceding year, and while there is a small excess in manufactures, every other department of our exports has fallen off quite largely-the forests, animals and their products, agricultural products, the fisheries, every one is diminished. There is another thing even more important, a point of which Sir Leonard Tilley took good note when he anticipated the decline coming in 1883, and that is the probable great decrease in prices. We have had good times in Canada, marvellously good times. This is due to a variety of circumstances. The first is the one great general cause, the swing of the pendulum upwards, which is world-wide. The second cause has been the war between Spain and the United States. Then there are the war in the Transvaal, the good crops and the Yukon, with its enormous development. And lastly, there is the enormous increase in prices. Prices, since these hon. gentlemen came into power, have advanced 20 per cent according to Bradstreet's table-from 68 to 88. That state of affairs is not going to last long. At an early day we are going to see a change. The apparent shrinkage of the exports of this country and the shrinking prices that wTill accompany it will. 1 fear, bring a state of affairs worse than my hon. friend the Minister of Finance expects. I hope it may not be so. In that, I am sure, I voice the opinion of hon. gentlemen on this side. While hon. gentlemen opposite, when on this side, did take pleasure to a certain extent in pointing out all the losses, all the bad balances that took place in the history of Canada, I do not think there is a man on this side who will not rejoice to see the country prosperous even beyond the expectation of the hon. Minister of Finance.
